pos: n. (the Norse-founded city on the Shannon, a Munster see, and the place of the treaty of 1691)
etymology: Irish Luimneach, perhaps the bare spot or the marshy ground; the Norse called it Hlymrekr.
biblical_def: Limerick stands where the Shannon becomes tidal, a Norse trading town from the ninth century, taken by Brian Boru's people, walled by the Normans, and made a diocese at the synod of Rathbreasail. Its history is a history of walls. It was besieged in 1642, in 1650 by Ireton, in 1690 and again in 1691, when the surrender was sealed by the Treaty of Limerick promising the Catholics of Ireland the religious liberty they had enjoyed under Charles II. The Irish parliament refused to ratify the religious articles, and the penal laws followed instead; the broken treaty poisoned relations between the communions for two centuries, and the stone on which it was signed is still shown. The dictionary records Limerick for the lesson that a city's strength is never in its masonry and that a people's safety is never in a promise men are willing to break. Scripture praises the walls of Zion and tells the worshipper to walk about and count the towers, but the song that does so begins by naming where salvation actually comes from: God appoints the walls, and the city is compact and strong because he keeps it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a city as a large town with a corporation; a wall as a structure raised for defence; a bulwark as a rampart or means of protection; a tower as a lofty building; and compact as closely united.
webster_full: CITY, n. In a general sense, a large town; a large number of houses and inhabitants, established in one place; in a stricter sense, a corporate town.
WALL, n. A work or structure of stone, brick or other materials, raised to some height, and intended for a defence or security.
BULWARK, n. In fortification, a bastion or a rampart; a mound of earth round a place, capable of resisting cannon shot; a means of protection or safety.
TOWER, n. A building, either round or square, raised to a considerable elevation; a citadel; a fortress.
COMPACT, a. Closely and firmly united, as the particles of solid bodies; joined; held together.
corruption_summary: Norse-founded Shannon city and Munster see, besieged four times in fifty years, where the treaty of 1691 was signed and its religious articles then repudiated.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one order in which a city's defences may safely be praised. Isaiah names the builder before the bulwark: “We have a strong city; salvation will God appoint for walls and bulwarks” (Isa 26:1). Only after that may the worshipper do what the Psalter invites, “Walk about Zion, and go round about her: tell the towers thereof” (Psa 48:12), and look at the defences as a work of God rather than of engineers.

The live temptation is the one the Treaty of Limerick exposed, which is to trust a document or a rampart in place of integrity. Four sieges proved the walls breakable and one parliament proved the promise breakable. The Psalter tells the people to look hard at the fortifications precisely so that they may hand on a testimony about God: “Mark ye well her bulwarks, consider her palaces; that ye may tell it to the generation following” (Psa 48:13). What held Jerusalem together was never chiefly the stonework, for “Jerusalem is builded as a city that is compact together” (Psa 122:3) by the covenant that gathered its tribes to one house.

pos: n. (the walled merchant city of Connacht, whose collegiate church was governed by an elected warden outside any bishop's jurisdiction)
etymology: Irish Gaillimh, from the river name, said to mean stony; the Anglo-Norman town took the river's name.
biblical_def: Galway was a walled merchant city on the edge of Connacht, run by fourteen Anglo-Norman families who traded wine, salt and fish with Spain and Bordeaux and kept the Irish of the countryside at arm's length. Its church arrangement was unique in Ireland: in 1484 the citizens obtained from Innocent VIII a wardenship, by which the collegiate church of St Nicholas was governed by a warden and eight vicars elected annually by the corporation itself, exempt from the archbishop of Tuam. The arrangement outlasted the Reformation on both sides and was not abolished until 1831. The city's whole character was mercantile, and its laws on weights, measures and the inspection of wine casks were strict and enforced. The dictionary records Galway for the merchant's standard. Scripture speaks about balances more often and more severely than most readers expect, and it does so because weights are where a man's religion becomes public: a false balance is called an abomination to the LORD, and the just weight is called his delight.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a balance as a pair of scales for weighing; a weight as a mass used in weighing; just as equitable and exact; an abomination as that which is loathed; and a measure as the standard by which quantity is determined.
webster_full: BALANCE, n. A pair of scales for weighing commodities; an instrument for ascertaining the weight of bodies.
WEIGHT, n. A mass of iron, lead, brass or other metal, to be used for ascertaining the weight of other bodies.
JUST, a. Regular; orderly; due; suitable; conformed to rules; equitable; exact; honest in dealings.
ABOMINATION, n. Extreme hatred; detestation; the object of detestation, a common signification in Scripture.
MEASURE, n. The whole extent or dimensions of a thing; that by which extent or dimension is ascertained; a standard.
corruption_summary: Walled Connacht merchant city whose collegiate church was run by an annually elected warden exempt from Tuam, abolished only in 1831.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that honest measures are a matter of worship and not merely of commerce. Solomon states both halves: “A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight” (Pro 11:1), and repeats it so that no trader can plead ignorance, “Divers weights are an abomination unto the LORD; and a false balance is not good” (Pro 20:23).

The live temptation in a trading city is to keep two sets of standards, a strict one for the law courts and a loose one for the day's profit. The law attaches a promise about the land itself to the merchant's scales: “But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have: that thy days may be lengthened in the land” (Deu 25:15). Amos exposes the religious version of the fraud, men impatient for the sabbath to end so that trade can resume, “making the ephah small, and the shekel great, and falsifying the balances by deceit” (Amo 8:5). A corporation that elected its own warden had every opportunity to be scrupulous and every opportunity not to be.

pos: n. (the Norse city on the Suir, a Munster see united with Lismore in 1363)
etymology: Norse Veðrafjörðr, the ram or weather fjord; the Irish is Port Láirge, the harbour of the haunch.
biblical_def: Waterford is the oldest city in Ireland, founded by Norsemen about 914 at the head of a deep harbour on the Suir. Its bishops were at first consecrated at Canterbury; it became a Latin diocese at Rathbreasail, and in 1363 the impoverished see of Lismore, once the greatest school of the southern Irish church, was united to it. Strongbow landed near it in 1170 and Henry II came ashore there in 1171, so that the English conquest of Ireland began from Waterford quay. The city was loyal to the crown through the Middle Ages and then stubbornly Catholic through the Reformation, refusing the Prayer Book, closing its gates to Cromwell in 1649 and falling to Ireton in 1650. The dictionary records Waterford because its diocese illustrates the perennial want of the Irish church, which was never a want of fields but of harvesters. Lismore's school emptied; the parishes stayed. The Lord's own diagnosis of such a situation is given once and repeated, that the harvest is plenteous and the labourers are few, and the remedy he commands is prayer to the Lord of the harvest.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a harvest as the season of gathering ripe corn; a labourer as one who works at hard manual labor; plenteous as abundant and copious; to send forth as to dispatch; and a field as a piece of land under cultivation.
webster_full: HARVEST, n. The season of reaping and gathering in corn or other crops; the ripe corn or grain collected and secured in barns.
LABORER, n. One who labors in a toilsome occupation; a man who does work that requires little skill, as distinguished from an artisan.
PLENTEOUS, a. Abundant; copious; plentiful; sufficient for every purpose.
SEND, v.t. To cause to go or pass from one place to another; to dispatch on an errand or for a purpose.
FIELD, n. A piece of land enclosed for tillage or pasture; the ground where a battle is fought; any open space.
corruption_summary: Ireland's oldest city, a Norse foundation on the Suir and a Munster see to which the great school of Lismore was united in 1363.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the Lord's own account of every under-supplied field, which puts the shortage in the labour and not in the ground: “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37). The remedy he appoints is not a scheme but a petition, and it is a command: “Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest” (Mat 9:38).

The live temptation when a diocese is poor is to consolidate and call it strategy, which is what happened when Lismore was folded into Waterford. Sometimes that is prudence; it is never a substitute for men. Christ gave the same charge again when he sent out the seventy, “The harvest truly is great, but the labourers are few” (Luk 10:2), and he rebuked the instinct to postpone the work until conditions improve: “Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest” (Joh 4:35). A quay where two invasions landed was also a field already white.

pos: n. (the Wexford see founded by Maedoc, and the seat of Dermot MacMurrough, who brought the Normans into Ireland)
etymology: Irish Fearna, the place of alder trees, from fearn, an alder.
biblical_def: Ferns in north Wexford was founded as a monastery by Maedoc, also called Aidan, in the late sixth century, and became the see of the diocese of Ferns for the kingdom of Leinster. Its abbey and its kings were bound together closely and badly. Dermot MacMurrough, King of Leinster, rebuilt the abbey as an Augustinian house and was buried in its grounds; he is also the man who, driven out of Ireland in 1166, went to Henry II for help, brought the Normans in, and so began eight hundred years of English rule. The cathedral was burned in the wars that followed, rebuilt in part, and after the Reformation held by John Garvey among others before he went to Armagh. The dictionary records Ferns because it shows what happens when a church becomes a political property. A house endowed to buy a king's standing is a house with a price on it, and Christ's two cleansings of the temple are the standing judgment on that arrangement: his Father's house is not to be a house of merchandise, and the house of prayer is not to be made a den of thieves.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines merchandise as the objects of commerce; a den as a cave or lurking place; a thief as one who takes goods secretly; prayer as a solemn address to God; and to trust as to confide in.
webster_full: MERCHANDISE, n. The objects of commerce; wares, goods, commodities, whatever is usually bought or sold in trade.
DEN, n. A cave or hollow place in the earth, used as a lurking place for beasts; a cavern.
THIEF, n. One who secretly, unlawfully and feloniously takes the goods or personal effects of another.
PRAYER, n. A solemn address to the Supreme Being, consisting of adoration, confession of sin, supplication and thanksgiving.
TRUST, n. Confidence; a reliance or resting of the mind on the integrity, veracity or power of another.
corruption_summary: Wexford see of Maedoc, rebuilt and held by Dermot MacMurrough of Leinster, the king who brought the Normans into Ireland in 1169.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one purpose of a sanctuary, which Christ asserts by quoting Isaiah against the traders: “My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves” (Mat 21:13). Luke records the same charge in the same temple, “My house is the house of prayer: but ye have made it a den of thieves” (Luk 19:46), so that no one may treat the cleansing as a single loss of temper.

The live temptation at Ferns was the patron's, a king endowing an abbey while using the church as an instrument of his quarrels. Christ's earlier word puts the ownership of the building where it belongs and forbids its conversion into an asset: “make not my Father's house an house of merchandise” (Joh 2:16). Jeremiah had already answered the people who thought a building guaranteed them: “Trust ye not in lying words, saying, The temple of the LORD, The temple of the LORD” (Jer 7:4). Dermot's abbey did not save his kingdom, and his kingdom did not sanctify his abbey.

pos: n. (the east Cork see of Colman, whose bishop from 1734 was the philosopher George Berkeley)
etymology: Irish Cluain Uamha, the meadow of the cave, from cluain, a meadow, and uaimh, a cave.
biblical_def: Cloyne is a village in east Cork with a round tower and a small cathedral, the see of a diocese founded by Colman mac Léníne in the sixth century, united to Cork at intervals and separate again. Its best known bishop is George Berkeley, appointed in 1734, who had already written the philosophical works for which he is remembered and who then spent eighteen years in an obscure Irish diocese doing the ordinary work of it: he catechised, he set up a spinning school, he dosed his neighbours with tar water during an epidemic, he resided when most bishops did not, and he wrote on the economic misery of the country. He is the rare case of a first-rate metaphysician who was also a conscientious parish bishop. The dictionary records Cloyne for exactly that combination, and for the caution that belongs to it. Learning is a servant and never a master in the church. Paul does not forbid philosophy but warns that a man may be carried off as spoil by it, and the test he gives is simple and final: whether a thing is after Christ or only after the tradition of men.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines philosophy as the knowledge of natural causes; to spoil as to plunder; a rudiment as a first principle; inspiration as the supernatural influence by which Scripture was given; and to increase as to grow and augment.
webster_full: PHILOSOPHY, n. Literally, the love of wisdom; the knowledge of natural causes and effects; the science which treats of the operations of the mind, or of the first causes of things.
SPOIL, v.t. To plunder; to strip by violence; to rob; to seize by violence; to take away as plunder.
RUDIMENT, n. A first principle or element; the first slight appearance or beginning of any thing.
INSPIRATION, n. The supernatural influence of the Spirit of God on the human mind, by which the prophets and apostles were qualified to receive and communicate divine truth.
INCREASE, v.i. To become greater in bulk, quantity, number, value, degree or extent; to grow; to advance.
corruption_summary: East Cork see of Colman whose bishop from 1734 was George Berkeley, a first-rate philosopher who resided, catechised and worked the diocese.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that learning in the church is a servant with a master, and Scripture is not shy about the use of a trained mind: “A wise man will hear, and will increase learning” (Pro 1:5). The source of its authority, however, lies outside the scholar altogether, for “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine” (2Ti 3:16), and what it does for the unlearned it does directly: “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130).

The live temptation for a bishop who is also a philosopher runs both ways, toward neglecting the diocese for the system and toward letting the system govern the doctrine. Paul draws the line precisely where it belongs, not against thought but against captivity to it: “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ” (Col 2:8). Berkeley catechised children and made tar water for his neighbours, which is what the warning looks like when it is heeded.

pos: n. (the see on the Shannon above Lough Derg, the church of Lua, in the country of Brian Boru)
etymology: Irish Cill Dalúa, the church of Dalúa or Lua, a sixth-century monk of the Shannon islands.
biblical_def: Killaloe stands on the Shannon where the river leaves Lough Derg, a crossing and a fishery, and the church there was founded by Lua, whose tiny oratory was moved from an island when the river was dammed in the twentieth century. Flannan was its first bishop in the seventh century. The place rose with the Dal Cais and with Brian Boru, whose fort of Kincora stood above the ford, and the diocese of Killaloe was confirmed at Rathbreasail in 1111 covering most of Clare and parts of Tipperary and Offaly. Its cathedral, built about 1200 on the site of Brian's brother's church, still holds a Romanesque doorway and an Ogham-and-runic cross slab. The dictionary records Killaloe for its river. A church built where a great water leaves a lake is a natural pulpit for the thing Scripture says most often about grace: that it is a river making glad the city of God, that where the river comes everything lives, and that the water Christ gives becomes a well inside the man who drinks it. The alternative Scripture names is a hewn cistern that holds nothing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a river as a large stream of water flowing in a channel; a fountain as a spring or source of water; a cistern as an artificial reservoir; a well as a spring or a pit sunk for water; and to thirst as to feel want of drink.
webster_full: RIVER, n. A large stream of water flowing in a channel on land towards the ocean, a lake or another river.
FOUNTAIN, n. A spring, or source of water; properly, a spring or issuing of water from the earth; original; first principle or cause.
CISTERN, n. An artificial reservoir or receptacle for holding water, beer or other liquor, as in domestic uses.
WELL, n. A spring; a fountain; a pit or cylindrical hole sunk into the earth to such a depth as to reach a supply of water.
THIRST, n. A painful sensation of the throat occasioned by the want of drink; eager desire for any thing.
corruption_summary: Shannon see of Lua and Flannan in Brian Boru's country, confirmed as a diocese in 1111, with a Romanesque cathedral of about 1200.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the scriptural figure of grace as a river, which is always a river that arrives from elsewhere. The Psalmist puts it at the centre of the city: “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God” (Psa 46:4), and Ezekiel traces the effect of the water from the temple down a dead valley, “whithersoever the rivers shall come, shall live” (Eze 47:9).

The live temptation is the cistern, religion as a stored supply that a man keeps for himself and that slowly empties. Christ's promise at the well runs the opposite way, inward and then upward: the water he gives “shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (Joh 4:14). Jeremiah names the exchange that is always on offer and always a disaster: “they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water” (Jer 2:13). A diocese on a great river had the sermon in front of it every day.

pos: n. (the Roscommon see traced to Patrick and his disciple Assicus, covering parts of Connacht on both sides of the Shannon)
etymology: Irish Ail Finn, the clear rock or the rock of the spring, from ail, a rock.
biblical_def: Elphin is a village in Roscommon, the seat of a diocese whose foundation the Irish tradition traces to Patrick himself, who is said to have left his disciple Assicus, a worker in metal, as its first bishop. The diocese straddled the Shannon, taking in parts of Roscommon, Sligo and Galway, and it was always poor; in the eighteenth century its Church of Ireland bishops, Edward Synge among them, left careful reports on the destitution of the people and the scarcity of resident clergy. Its cathedral was small and was finally destroyed by a storm in 1957. The dictionary records Elphin because a poor and scattered diocese puts the test of a shepherd most plainly. Ezekiel's indictment of the shepherds of Israel is not that they taught error but that they fed themselves, left the diseased unstrengthened, the sick unhealed, the broken unbound and the lost unsought. Where a bishop could not be everywhere, the question was simply whether he went where the people were, and some did.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a shepherd as one who tends sheep; to feed as to supply with nourishment; diseased as disordered in body; to bind up as to confine with a bandage; and to rule as to govern.
webster_full: SHEPHERD, n. A man employed in tending, feeding and guarding sheep in the field; also, a pastor, a minister of the gospel.
FEED, v.t. To give food to; to supply with provisions; to nourish; to supply with any thing of which there is continual consumption.
DISEASED, a. Disordered; distempered; afflicted with disease or sickness.
BIND, v.t. To tie together, or confine with a cord or any thing that is flexible; to bind up a wound.
RULE, v.t. To govern; to control the will and actions of others, either by arbitrary power or by laws.
corruption_summary: Poor Connacht see traced to Patrick and Assicus, straddling the Shannon, whose eighteenth-century bishops reported on destitution and absent clergy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Ezekiel's test of a pastor, which asks what he does rather than what he believes. The charge is laid in the form of a question: “Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?” (Eze 34:2), and the particulars follow with no room to hide, “neither have ye sought that which was lost” (Eze 34:4).

The live temptation in a poor diocese is to accept absence as inevitable, and then to call the absence economy. Christ's own restoration of a fallen minister came with the same duty attached three times over: “He saith unto him, Feed my sheep” (Joh 21:16). The people's part is to submit to men who genuinely do that work, and the writer to the Hebrews gives both the ground and the warning: “for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account” (Heb 13:17). An account rendered for a flock nobody visited is the thing Elphin's better bishops feared.

pos: n. (the small Sligo see founded by Nathy, long the poorest diocese in Connacht)
etymology: Irish Achadh Conaire, Conaire's field, from achadh, a field.
biblical_def: Achonry is a townland in County Sligo with the remains of a small cathedral, the seat of a diocese founded, the tradition says, when Patrick gave the place to Nathy, called Cruimthir Nathy, in the fifth century. It was recognised as a diocese at the synod of Kells in 1152 and has always been among the smallest and poorest in Ireland; it had at times no cathedral in use, no episcopal residence and very little revenue, and it was repeatedly proposed for union with its neighbours. It survives still as a diocese with its see at Ballaghaderreen. The dictionary records Achonry for the smallest of all the lessons the Irish sees teach, which is that God is not embarrassed by a small work. The prophet to the returned exiles put the question to men discouraged by the modest scale of the second temple, who hath despised the day of small things, and the answer given was a promise that the latter house would have greater glory than the first. The increase in such work is never the builder's to supply.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to despise as to contemn and scorn; small as of little size or importance; glory as splendor and honor; to plant as to set in the earth for growth; and increase as augmentation and growth.
webster_full: DESPISE, v.t. To contemn; to scorn; to disdain; to have the lowest opinion of.
SMALL, a. Slender; thin; fine; of little size; of little moment, weight or importance.
GLORY, n. Brightness; luster; splendor; praise ascribed in adoration; honorable fame; the divine presence.
PLANT, v.t. To put in the ground and cover, as seed for growth; to set in the earth for propagation.
INCREASE, n. Augmentation; a growing larger; that which is added; produce; profit.
corruption_summary: The smallest and poorest Connacht see, founded by Nathy and recognised at Kells in 1152, repeatedly proposed for union and still surviving.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God does not measure a work as men measure it. Zechariah puts the rebuke to the discouraged builders as a question: “For who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10), and Haggai, speaking to men who wept at the modesty of the second temple, promised more than they had lost, “The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former” (Hag 2:9).

The live temptation with a small charge is to think the smallness is the problem. Paul assigns the labour and withholds the credit in a single sentence: “I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1Co 3:6), which means that a tiny diocese and a great one depend on the same thing and neither can manufacture it. The Psalter describes the work itself as sowing with tears and promises the harvest without naming the scale: “He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing” (Psa 126:6). Achonry has gone forth weeping for fifteen centuries.

Greek phuteuo (G5452) — to plant; “I have planted, Apollos watered”, 1 Corinthians 3:6.
Greek auxano (G0837) — to cause to grow; “but God gave the increase”, 1 Corinthians 3:6.
Hebrew zera (H2233) — seed; “bearing precious seed”, Psalm 126:6.

pos: n. (the Carlow see of Laserian, where a synod about 630 accepted the Roman reckoning of Easter for the southern Irish)
etymology: Irish Leithghlinn, the half glen, from leath, half, and gleann, a glen.
biblical_def: Old Leighlin in County Carlow was a monastery founded by Gobban and ruled by Laserian, also called Molaise, in the early seventh century. Its importance is that a synod met there about 630, in the middle of the long Irish quarrel over the date of Easter, and decided for the Roman computation, so that the southern half of Ireland conformed while the north and the Columban houses held out for generations more. Laserian is said to have gone to Rome to settle the question and to have come back as papal legate. The diocese of Leighlin was confirmed at Rathbreasail and united with Ferns in 1600. The dictionary records Leighlin for the use and the limits of a synod. Scripture commends the taking of counsel in plain terms, saying that where no counsel is the people fall and that in the multitude of counsellors there is safety, and it promises Christ's presence to a gathering of two or three in his name. What it never does is make an assembly the author of what it decides.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines counsel as advice and deliberation; a counsellor as one who gives advice; to establish as to make firm; to assemble as to meet together; and to forsake as to abandon or desert.
webster_full: COUNSEL, n. Advice; opinion or instruction given upon request or otherwise, for directing the judgment or conduct of another; deliberation.
COUNSELLOR, n. Any person who gives advice; but properly one who is authorized by natural relationship, or by birth, office or profession, to advise another.
ESTABLISH, v.t. To set and fix firmly or unalterably; to settle permanently; to confirm; to ratify.
ASSEMBLE, v.i. To meet or come together; to convene, as a number of individuals.
FORSAKE, v.t. To quit or leave entirely; to desert; to abandon; to depart from.
corruption_summary: Carlow see of Laserian, where a synod about 630 brought the southern Irish to the Roman reckoning of Easter while the north held out.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the proper use of common counsel, which Scripture commends without apology: “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14), and again with the positive side stated, “Without counsel purposes are disappointed: but in the multitude of counsellors they are established” (Pro 15:22). A synod at Leighlin was doing what an Irish monastery ought to have done with a disputed question.

The live temptation is to make the assembly the author rather than the servant of the truth it declares, and the Easter controversy shows what follows: two Irish churches keeping different feasts and each claiming the authority of a council. What Christ promises a gathering is his presence, not his signature on whatever it resolves: “For where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Mat 18:20). And the duty of gathering at all stands whatever the date of the feast: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25).

pos: n. (Llantwit Major in Glamorgan, Illtud's monastic school, called the first and greatest school of the British church)
etymology: Welsh Llanilltud Fawr, the great church enclosure of Illtud, from llan, a church enclosure.
biblical_def: Llantwit Major in the Vale of Glamorgan held the monastic school of Illtud, founded in the late fifth or early sixth century, and the Welsh tradition makes it the first school of the British church and the training place of the men who carried the faith across the Severn Sea and into Brittany. Samson of Dol, Paul Aurelian and Gildas are all named as its pupils, and David of Wales is claimed for it as well. Illtud is described by Gildas's generation as the teacher of almost all Britain, a man learned in the Scriptures and in the arts, and the school combined manual labour, farming and study. Its churchyard holds one of the finest collections of early Christian carved crosses in Britain. The dictionary records Llantwit because its whole significance is in what it handed on. Not one book of Illtud's survives; what survives is a generation of men who were taught by him and who taught others. That is the mechanism Paul commanded and the Psalter describes: one generation praising God's works to another and declaring his mighty acts.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a school as a place of instruction; a generation as a single succession of men; to declare as to make known; to read as to utter written words; and a teacher as one who instructs.
webster_full: SCHOOL, n. A place or house in which persons are instructed in arts, science, languages or any species of learning.
GENERATION, n. A single succession in natural descent, as the children of the same parents; the people of the same period.
DECLARE, v.t. To make known; to tell explicitly; to manifest or communicate plainly to others by words.
READ, v.t. To utter or pronounce written or printed words, letters or characters in the proper order; to peruse.
TEACHER, n. One who teaches or instructs; an instructor; a preceptor; one who instructs others in religion.
corruption_summary: Illtud's monastic school in Glamorgan, the first great school of the British church, which trained Samson, Paul Aurelian and Gildas.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Llantwit embodies, which is that the church's learning travels through persons. Paul commands the chain and shows four links of it at once: what Timothy heard is to be committed “to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2), and Christ's gift to his church is a list of men and not of institutions, “and some, pastors and teachers” (Eph 4:11).

The live temptation is to measure a school by its output of books, by which measure Illtud left nothing at all. The older and better measure is public reading and public hearing, commanded for Israel at the feast: “thou shalt read this law before all Israel in their hearing” (Deu 31:11). The Psalter puts the whole aim of such a school in one line, where the work of transmission is itself worship: “One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts” (Psa 145:4). Samson, Paul Aurelian and Gildas were Illtud's publications.
